exam: A 45‑year‑old woman presents with sudden ‘worst headache’ and neck stiffness – what is your immediate diagnostic step? — Obtain non‑contrast CT head; if negative, perform lumbar puncture.

You find a 6 mm anterior communicating artery aneurysm on CTA in a hypertensive patient – what factors influence the decision for clipping vs coiling? — Size, neck morphology, available expertise, and patient stability guide choice; coiling preferred if endovascular services exist.

During resuscitation, blood pressure spikes to 180/110 mmHg – how do you manage it and why? — Use IV labetalol or nicardipine to keep systolic <140 mmHg, preventing re‑bleeding while avoiding hypotension.

A patient with known HIV presents with SAH – what additional cause should you consider? — HIV‑associated vasculitis or mycotic aneurysm; obtain blood cultures and consider broad‑spectrum antibiotics if infection suspected.
What bedside sign helps differentiate SAH from meningitis? — Presence of photophobia and neck stiffness in SAH is often abrupt; meningitis usually has fever and gradual onset.

If CT angiography is unavailable, what is the next best step to locate the aneurysm? — Arrange transfer for conventional digital subtraction angiography or, if impossible, refer urgently for surgical exploration based on clinical picture.
Why is nimodipine given after SAH but not before repair? — It prevents vasospasm and delayed ischemia post‑hemorrhage; it does not affect aneurysm stability.

A patient develops worsening consciousness after SAH – what complication should you suspect and how to confirm? — Hydrocephalus; confirm with bedside ultrasound of ventricles or CT showing enlarged ventricles.
ai.title: Intracranial Aneurysm
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: A focal dilation of a cerebral artery that can rupture causing subarachnoid hemorrhage. Recognise risk factors, presentation and limited investigations in low‑resource settings to guide urgent management.

sections.p: An intracranial aneurysm is a saccular outpouching of a cerebral artery wall, most often at arterial bifurcations in the circle of Willis. It may be silent or present with sentinel headache, focal deficits, or catastrophic subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH).

b: Most common sites: anterior communicating artery, posterior communicating artery, middle cerebral artery bifurcation
Size predicts rupture: <5 mm low risk, 5–7 mm moderate, >7 mm high
sections.p: Risk factors are divided into non‑modifiable (age > 40, female sex, family history, congenital connective‑tissue disorders) and modifiable (hypertension, smoking, heavy alcohol, HIV, TB meningitis). In low‑resource settings, untreated hypertension and HIV‑related vasculitis are common precipitants.

b: Look for meningeal signs (neck rigidity, Kernig’s sign)
Check for focal deficits (cranial nerve palsy, hemiparesis)
Assess blood pressure – hypertensive spikes raise rupture risk
sections.p: Patients may present with a sudden ‘worst‑ever’ headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, or focal neurologic loss if the aneurysm compresses adjacent structures. A sentinel leak can cause a transient headache days before rupture.

t.b: Is there acute SAH? – Hyperdense fluid in sulci confirms hemorrhage; if negative but suspicion high, proceed to lumbar puncture.
Does CSF show xanthochromia? – Positive xanthochromia indicates SAH when imaging is unavailable.
Where is the aneurysm and what is its size? – Shows location, morphology; essential for surgical planning. If unavailable, refer for conventional angiography when possible.
Gold‑standard anatomy for endovascular coiling – Used when CTA/MRA not definitive or for treatment planning.

b: Maintain systolic BP < 140 mmHg using IV labetalol or nicardipine; avoid rapid drops.
Give analgesia and anti‑emetics; avoid NSAIDs that increase bleeding risk.
Treat hydrocephalus with external ventricular drain if signs of raised intracranial pressure.
Arrange urgent transfer to centre with neurosurgical capability.
sections.p: Stabilise the patient, control blood pressure, prevent re‑bleeding, and arrange definitive repair (surgical clipping or endovascular coiling). In low‑resource hospitals, focus on supportive care and timely transfer.

b: Migraine with aura – gradual onset, reversible visual symptoms, no meningeal signs.
Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis – often in pregnancy, shows venous infarcts on imaging.
Pituitary apoplexy – sudden headache with ophthalmoplegia, pituitary mass on imaging.
sections.p: Other causes of sudden severe headache or focal deficits.

b: CT may miss SAH within first 6 h if scan quality poor; lumbar puncture needed.
Xanthochromia may be absent if LP performed <12 h after bleed.
sections.p: Imaging and CSF findings may be falsely normal early after bleed.

b: First step in suspected SAH: non‑contrast CT head.
If CT negative and high suspicion, perform lumbar puncture.
Key factor for treatment urgency: aneurysm size > 7 mm or symptomatic.
sections.p: Exam questions often test your ability to prioritise actions and differentiate rupture from mimics.

whenToSeekHelp: Loss of consciousness or worsening neurological status
